newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Twists of fate dog Britain's Hong Kong envoy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Twists of fate dog Britain's Hong Kong envoy.

text.p: Chris Patten, Britain's last governor of Hong Kong, may have missed his moment once or twice back home, but one moment he does not intend to pass up is the colony's handover to China, even if Beijing might prefer he did.
Describing his current job as one of the most exciting and rewarding of his career, Patten, 53, told Reuters he would see it through to the last minute of British rule.

"I hope people will think I did my best to stand up for Hong Kong...that I did my best to ensure Hong Kong was an open, decent, free, successful society," said Patten, who has retained a high popularity rating, with two-thirds to three-quarters of citizens approving of him.
At midnight on June 30, London hands the colony back to China after more than a century and a half of colonial rule.
PATTEN FRETS FOR HONG KONG'S FREEDOM AND PROSPERITY

Patten leaves the terrotiry worrying that Chinese leaders will tinker with the smoothly running engine that has made Hong Kong the world's eighth largest trading economy and fifth largest banking centre.
He said his preoccupation had been to live up to the promises that were made to Hong Kong's 6.4 million people in the Sino-British handover treaty.
The treaty guaranteed Hong Kong's freewheeling capitalist system would remain unchanged for 50 years after the territory becomes a highly autonomous part of China.
In his crusade to defend this pledge, Patten upset Chinese mandarins, as well as Hong Kong tycoons who sought favour in Beijing while having a foreign passport in their back pocket.
"People do not like the idea that the freedoms they enjoy and exercise sensibly today will be snatched away from them," Patten wrote in a recent newspaper column.
POLITICAL FIGHTER CURSED BY MISSED MOMENTS
Deep down, the Patten who loves a political fight at the hustings, the Patten once tipped as a future prime minister, might wish he was not here at all.

The moderate Tory was sidelined by the spectacular rise of another politician of his generation, John Major, who replaced Margaret Thatcher as Conservative Party premier in 1990, till his May 1 election defeat by Labour leader Tony Blair.
When Patten, credited with masterminding Major's unexpected general election victory in 1992, lost his parliamentary seat, Major quickly offered the party chairman the key Hong Kong post.

Within weeks of his arrival in Britain's last Asian outpost, Patten found himself on a path to confrontation with China which furiously rejected democratic reforms the British were planning in response to populist demands.
Now, with the Conservatives routed this month and about to put the leadership up for grabs, he is again missing the race.
"I wouldn't advise anybody to put any money on me. One of the things which I lack in the leadership stake is a seat in the Commons," Patten said after Major's polls defeat this month.
"The only plans I have at present are to take six or seven months off after the handover of Hong Kong to write a book about Asia and Europe," he said.
WITH A COMMON TOUCH, PATTEN MOVED DEMOCRACY FORWARD

Abandoning the pomp and tradition of a governorial uniform with a feathered cap, Patten, the 28th Governor in the colony's 156 year history, arrived with the job of steering the territory towards Chinese rule.
He got down assiduously to the task, and for good measure rammed through electoral reforms, giving birth to Hong Kong's first fully elected legislature.
Chinese officials retaliated by reviling him as a serpent, a villain, and a "prostitute for a thousand generations", and made plans to dismantle his reforms this July 1.
The territory faces a step backward in terms of democracy and civil rights, but the Patten-era legacy is profound.

"Like the rest of Asia, Hong Kong has gone through a historic transformation over the last 20 years. And it's gone through a political transformation too. It's more open. And the government's more accountable. Quite right," Patten said in a recent radio broadcast.
"I happen to think myself that Hong Kong needs governing with a light touch... You can't turn the clock back on what Hong Kong has become, any more than you can reverse the countdown.
"I hope that some of China's advisers will stop seeing Hong Kong in terms of struggle, will stop tilting against so-called British windmills."
POPULAR STYLE DIFFERED FROM CHINESE OFFICIALS
Patten's man-of-the-people, walkabout style contrasts with the secretive, withdrawn Chinese officials stationed at China's mission in Hong Kong.

He enlivened the Hong Kong political debate, referring to a new legislature that China has appointed for Hong Kong as an "echo chamber", and describing Hong Kong itself as a new car -- "if it ain't broke, don't fix it".

"Hong Kong is like a Rolls-Royce. All you need to do if you're in charge is slip into the drivers's seat, switch on the ignition, and away you go. I don't quite see the point of lifting the bonnet to tinker with the engine," he said.
Amid speculation on his political future, apart from the book, Patten plans "some months recharging my batteries" and tending his garden at a country home in France.
